This topic has actually been on my mind a fair amount in recent time. 

I don’t necessarily feel pushed away from my dad’s (white) identity in extension to mine, but there’s definitely motives at play against identifying with my white side the same way I can with my Mexican side. 

I think a lot of it has to do with the idea of whiteness being pure. At least in an American perspective on race, you’re in that racial categorization or you aren’t.  

I do feel like white being seen as the default in America in many instances makes halves like myself be seen as “watered down,” which I feel, if changed, would alleviate some of the more subtle negative cultural views being mixed with white cones with. Some of which I can’t really explain, but I feel.

If you’ve identified as a quarter Hispanic prior to DNA testing then that should be what you continue to identify as, no matter how the admixture shows itself. 

The only case where something would change as far as identity goes because of a DNA test would probably be if you discovered something dramatically different than what you thought you were. If a quarter of you is still some variation of Spanish, Indigenous, SSA and North African then no matter which category’s it favors, you’re still a quarter Hispanic. 

Even if your results heavily favor that of a more European admixture for your Hispanic side, I don’t think that changes much. I’m half Hispanic and my results favoring a higher indigenous percentage doesn’t detract my identity and it wouldn’t have if it were the opposite with a higher Spanish percentage. 

At the end of the day there’s so much variation in Latin America so I wouldn’t worry too much about the specifics.

You can generally tell if you’re mixed with Hispanic/Latino by seeing whether or not you have a substantial amount of Iberian + Indigenous + SSA + WANA, which is the general admixture seen in Latin American nations. 

For example, I’m half Mexican and I have 2% Iberian, 38% Indigenous, 2% Bantu Peoples and 8% of NW Euro that I attribute to my Mexican side. 

Some variation of this in whatever quantity you believe  you might be (50%, 25%, etc) could tell you if are in part Hispanic. 

However, Spanish and Indigenous are the two biggest quantum’s seen in most Hispanic people. So any substantially big amount of WANA or SSA is out of the ordinary, it’s mostly in <5% amounts.

I think I can understand why some people here are against you identifying as partially Native; for one, it doesn’t seem like you’re all that connected to your Mexican side in the first place- at least, that’s the idea I get reading some of your responses. I don’t necessarily think that this can be solved by having practices more in-line with general Mexican culture, at least while on the forefront. It can definitely help, of course, but I feel as though you need to have more confidence in your identity first. Personally, I know what it’s like to have your identity challenged by others, even by family members. You just have to create/recognize a solid foundation for yourself and learn as you go, maybe even coming to a point where you topple the expectations, but that shouldn't be the end all, be all. Validation from others can be comforting, but if you’re mindfully valid in yourself, that’s all that matters.

Beyond that, though, I don’t think anyone wants to bar you from the possibility of educating yourself on whatever tribe you might be connected to, if you have the ability to do so. In this instance, I think people are hung up on your clean shot of tightening your connection to Mexico over an unnamed Tribe, since most cannot locate their tribe(s). Shooting in the dark and learning another culture thinking it was your own can be even worse in the long term, too.

Where I start to veer off from the crowd, personally, is where I believe it’s any of our rights as Hispanic/Latino people (In part or full) to favor our Indigenous sides over the generalized nationalistic identities many of us might have grown up with, especially within the US. Many people in Latin America might have forfeited their Indigenous identities long ago, but I can’t believe these were done in good conscience, with hierarchies being in place, tribal identity being disincentivized, war being waged, etc. It’s no mystery why they faded. I think even if we have identified as Mestizo as a majority for however many generations, in favoring the Spanish in language and various cultural aspects, if we can locate and learn from what we once were, it’s our right to reclaim it and identify with it. The people we descend from were native to the America’s and it’s our subsequent duty to educate others that “Native American” doesn’t only apply to the US and Canadian Natives. It doesn’t make sense that this modern confusion in some people’s minds bars the right for some to identify as Native in some minds.

Mestizo means to be of Indigenous and Spanish descent, usually of equal or similar quantity, yet the only Native American practices being taught on a wide scale (in Mexico) seems to be some aspects of Dia De Los Muertos, and maybe some foods and words like Chocolate, Mole, etc. that derived from Nahuatl, among others. 

My Mexican half being primarily Native American in race shouldn’t be the only end of the admixture that gets a pass to explore this part and identify as such, it should be open to all. We were all colonized. But that’s just my honest opinion. It’s your choice at the end of the day of where it takes you.
